entries.name: The Table designates the materials it lists as hazardous materials
entries.evidence: (a) The Hazardous Materials Table (Table) in this section designates the materials listed therein as hazardous materials for the purpose of transportation of those materials. For each listed material, the Table identifies the hazard class or specifies that the material is forbidden in transportation, and gives the proper shipping name or directs the user to the preferred proper shipping name. In addition, the Table specifies or references requirements in this subchapter pertaining to labeling, packaging, quantity limits aboard aircraft and stowage of hazardous materials aboard vessels.
entries.note: The whole grid rests on this sentence: a material is a hazardous material for transportation because the Table lists it, and the Table is also where its class, its proper shipping name, its labelling, its packaging, its aircraft quantity limits and its vessel stowage are stated or referenced. A test must show that a material not listed in the Table is not designated by this section.

entries.evidence: (b) Column 1: Symbols. Column 1 of the Table contains six symbols (“ + ”, “A”, “D”, “G”, “I” and “W”) as follows:

entries.name: Column 1 symbol “+”
entries.evidence: (1) The plus (+) sign fixes the proper shipping name, hazard class and packing group for that entry without regard to whether the material meets the definition of that class, packing group or any other hazard class definition. When the plus sign is assigned to a proper shipping name in Column (1) of the § 172.101 Table, it means that the material is known to pose a risk to humans. When a plus sign is assigned to mixtures or solutions containing a material where the hazard to humans is significantly different from that of the pure material or where no hazard to humans is posed, the material may be described using an alternative shipping name that represents the hazards posed by the material. An appropriate alternate proper shipping name and hazard class may be authorized by the Associate Administrator.
entries.note: The symbol fixes the proper shipping name, hazard class and packing group. None of the seven mapped rows carries it, so a test must exercise it against a row outside this slice or against a constructed entry; what the mapped rows show is only that the symbol is absent.

entries.name: Column 2 lists the proper shipping names, in Roman type only
entries.evidence: (c) Column 2: Hazardous materials descriptions and proper shipping names. Column 2 lists the hazardous materials descriptions and proper shipping names of materials designated as hazardous materials. Modification of a proper shipping name may otherwise be required or authorized by this section. Proper shipping names are limited to those shown in Roman type (not italics).
entries.note: The sentence that makes typography normative: “Proper shipping names are limited to those shown in Roman type (not italics).” The rule is readable; applying it to a particular column 2 cell is not, because the `ecfr-xml` adapter flattens <E T="03">. entries.name: A proper shipping name may be inflected and respelled
entries.evidence: (1) Proper shipping names may be used in the singular or plural and in either capital or lower case letters. Words may be alternatively spelled in the same manner as they appear in the ICAO Technical Instructions or the IMDG Code. For example “aluminum” may be spelled “aluminium” and “sulfur” may be spelled “sulphur”. However, the word “inflammable” may not be used in place of the word “flammable”.
entries.note: Singular or plural, either case, ICAO or IMDG spelling — and “inflammable” is refused outright. A test must show the refusal as well as the three permissions.

entries.name: Words in italics are not part of the proper shipping name
entries.evidence: (2) Punctuation marks and words in italics are not part of the proper shipping name, but may be used in addition to the proper shipping name. The word “or” in italics indicates that there is a choice of terms in the sequence that may alternately be used as the proper shipping name or as part of the proper shipping name, as appropriate. For example, for the hazardous materials description “Carbon dioxide, solid or Dry ice” either “Carbon dioxide, solid” or “Dry ice” may be used as the proper shipping name; and for the hazardous materials description “Articles, pressurized pneumatic or hydraulic,” either “Articles, pressurized pneumatic” or “Articles, pressurized hydraulic” may be used as the proper shipping name.
entries.note: This is the rule the protocol's `formatting: "rendered-page-required"` exists for. It also fixes what an italic “or” does: it offers a choice of names. A test must show both halves — that italic qualifying words drop out, and that an italic “or” splits one cell into two usable names.

entries.evidence: (10) Mixtures and solutions. (i) A mixture or solution meeting the definition of one or more hazard class that is not identified specifically by name, comprised of a single predominant hazardous material identified in the Table by technical name and one or more hazardous and/or non-hazardous material, must be described using the proper shipping name of the hazardous material and the qualifying word “mixture” or “solution”, as appropriate, unless— (A) Except as provided in § 172.101(i)(4) the packaging specified in Column 8 is inappropriate to the physical state of the material; (B) The shipping description indicates that the proper shipping name applies only to the pure or technically pure hazardous material; (C) The hazard class, packing group, or subsidiary hazard of the mixture or solution is different from that specified for the entry; (D) There is a significant change in the measures to be taken in emergencies; (E) The material is identified by special provision in Column 7 of the § 172.101 Table as a material poisonous by inhalation; however, it no longer meets the definition of poisonous by inhalation or it falls within a different hazard zone than that specified in the special provision; or (F) The material can be appropriately described by a shipping name that describes its intended application, such as “Coating solution”, “Extracts, flavoring” or “Compound, cleaning liquid.”. entries.name: A material determined to be of another class is described by that class's name
entries.evidence: (12) Except when the proper shipping name in the Table is preceded by a plus (+)— (i) If it is specifically determined that a material meets the definition of a hazard class, packing group or hazard zone, other than the class, packing group or hazard zone shown in association with the proper shipping name, or does not meet the defining criteria for a subsidiary hazard shown in Column 6 of the Table, the material shall be described by an appropriate proper shipping name listed in association with the correct hazard class, packing group, hazard zone, or subsidiary hazard for the material. (ii) Generic or n.o.s. descriptions. If an appropriate technical name is not shown in the Table, selection of a proper shipping name shall be made from the generic or n.o.s. descriptions corresponding to the specific hazard class, packing group, hazard zone, or subsidiary hazard, if any, for the material. The name that most appropriately describes the material shall be used, e.g., an alcohol not listed by its technical name in the Table shall be described as “Alcohol, n.o.s.” rather than “Flammable liquid, n.o.s.” Some mixtures may be more appropriately described according to their application, such as “Coating solution” or “Extracts, liquid, for flavor or aroma,” rather than by an n.o.s. entry, such as “Flammable liquid, n.o.s.” It should be noted, however, that an n.o.s. description as a proper shipping name may not provide sufficient information for shipping papers and package markings. Under the provisions of subparts C and D of this part, the technical name of one or more constituents that makes the product a hazardous material may be required in association with the proper shipping name. (iii) Multiple hazard materials. If a material meets the definition of more than one hazard class, and is not identified in the Table specifically by name (e.g., acetyl chloride), the hazard class of the material shall be determined by using the precedence specified in § 173.2a of this subchapter, and an appropriate shipping description (e.g., “Flammable liquid, corrosive n.o.s.”) shall be selected as described in paragraph (c)(12)(ii) of this section. entries.note: Two ways to satisfy it — corrosion-resistant steel, or protection against corrosion — which is a disjunction a test must show both arms of. It binds transportation by aircraft and nothing else, and that is stated in § 172.102(b)(2) rather than here: the paragraph's own text says nothing about mode. `enabledBy` is where the map records it, which is H3's claim.

entries.name: Special provision A10: Aluminium construction materials must resist corrosion
entries.evidence: A10 When aluminum or aluminum alloy construction materials are used, they must be resistant to corrosion.
entries.note: Conditional on aluminium being used at all; it forbids no material. It binds transportation by aircraft and nothing else, and that is stated in § 172.102(b)(2) rather than here: the paragraph's own text says nothing about mode. `enabledBy` is where the map records it, which is H3's claim.

entries.name: Special provision B2: Seven named cargo tanks are not authorized
entries.evidence: B2 MC 300, MC 301, MC 302, MC 303, MC 305, and MC 306 and DOT 406 cargo tanks are not authorized.
entries.note: A closed list of seven specifications, and three other B codes in the same run print nearly the same sentence with a different list; the quote is held to this paragraph by its citation and its own words (0030). Bulk packagings only, and not UN or IM portable tanks or IBCs, which § 172.102(b)(3) states and this paragraph does not.

entries.name: Special provision B16: The lading must be covered with nitrogen or another inert material
entries.evidence: B16 The lading must be completely covered with nitrogen, inert gas or other inert materials.
entries.note: One sentence, three named alternatives, the last of them open (“other inert materials”). That openness is a property of a material and not a blank in the rule, so gate 1 stops it and no assertion entry is owed. Bulk packagings only, and not UN or IM portable tanks or IBCs, which § 172.102(b)(3) states and this paragraph does not.

entries.name: Special provision N40: three packagings are not authorized
entries.evidence: N40 This material is not authorized in the following packagings: a. A combination packaging consisting of a 4G fiberboard box with inner receptacles of glass or earthenware; b. A single packaging of a 4C2 sift-proof, natural wood box; or c. A composite packaging 6PG2 (glass, porcelain or stoneware receptacles within a fiberboard box).
entries.note: A prohibition with a closed list of three packagings, printed as a lead-in and three lettered items under one designation. The whole rule is one contiguous span because the corpus prints the four paragraphs consecutively; quoting only the lead-in would have left the prohibition empty. It binds non-bulk packagings only (§ 172.102(b)(5)), and it is one of the two modal codes on the Alkali metal amalgam row.

entries.name: Special provision W31: non-bulk packagings must be hermetically sealed
entries.evidence: W31 Non-bulk packagings must be hermetically sealed.
entries.note: Six words, and every one of them about packaging rather than about water. That it applies only to transportation by water is § 172.102(b)(9)'s, and it is the clearest instance in the slice of a rule whose applicability is nowhere in its own text.

entries.name: Special provision TP1: the maximum degree of filling
entries.evidence: TP1 The maximum degree of filling must not exceed the degree of filling determined by the following: Where: tr is the maximum mean bulk temperature during transport, and tf is the temperature in degrees celsius of the liquid during filling.
entries.note: The rule is a formula, and the corpus serves the formula as a <MATH> element whose only text is the variable glosses: the prose says “determined by the following:” and then the expression itself is not in the extraction at all. So the paragraph is readable and the rule is not, which is exactly what `beyondAdapter` records (0004). The entry is still cited and still quoted — it is unreadable, not uncitable — and an engine declines it `MissingRulesData` naming the reader that failed.

entries.name: Special provision TP2: the maximum degree of filling, with a coefficient of expansion
entries.evidence: TP2 a. The maximum degree of filling must not exceed the degree of filling determined by the following: Where: tr is the maximum mean bulk temperature during transport, tf is the temperature in degrees celsius of the liquid during filling, and α is the mean coefficient of cubical expansion of the liquid between the mean temperature of the liquid during filling (tf) and the maximum mean bulk temperature during transportation (tr) both in degrees celsius. b. For liquids transported under ambient conditions α may be calculated using the formula:
entries.note: Two formulae rather than TP1's one — the degree of filling, and a calculation of the mean coefficient of cubical expansion for liquids carried at ambient conditions — and neither is in the extraction. Same verdict as TP1 and a wider one: an engine that implemented TP1 from a rendered page would still owe TP2 a second reading.

entries.name: Special provision TP7: the vapour space must be purged of air
entries.evidence: TP7 The vapor space must be purged of air by nitrogen or other means.
entries.note: “by nitrogen or other means” leaves the means open and states the result it is measured by — the vapour space is purged of air — so the openness is in how the duty is discharged and not in whether it is. Gate 1 returns no blank and the entry stays an operation.

entries.name: Special provision TP33: portable tanks for granular, powdered and molten solids

ambiguity.question: A solid carried above its melting point may go in a tank conforming to T4 or T7 “unless a tank with more stringent requirements for minimum shell thickness, maximum allowable working pressure, pressure-relief devices or bottom outlets are assigned”. The four dimensions are named and no rule orders them, so where an assigned instruction is more stringent in one and less in another — T9 assigns a 6 mm shell where T4 assigns § 178.274(d)(2), and bottom openings “Prohibited for liquids” where T4 assigns § 178.275(d)(3) — the corpus does not say which tank instruction applies. The Alkali metal amalgam row carries TP33 and T9 together, so the question is reachable inside this slice and not a constructed one.

entries.evidence: TP33 The portable tank instruction assigned for this substance applies for granular and powdered solids and for solids which are filled and discharged at temperatures above their melting point which are cooled and transported as a solid mass. Solid substances transported or offered for transport above their melting point are authorized for transportation in portable tanks conforming to the provisions of portable tank instruction T4 for solid substances of packing group III or T7 for solid substances of packing group II, unless a tank with more stringent requirements for minimum shell thickness, maximum allowable working pressure, pressure-relief devices or bottom outlets are assigned in which case the more stringent tank instruction and special provisions shall apply. Filling limits must be in accordance with portable tank special provision TP3. Solids meeting the definition of an elevated temperature material must be transported in accordance with the applicable requirements of this subchapter.
entries.note: The longest provision in the slice and the only one that reads two other provisions by name. Its filling limits sentence points at TP3, which no mapped row invokes and which this map therefore records as an unanswered pointer rather than an entry.

entries.name: IB2 authorises three families of IBC
entries.evidence: IB2 | Authorized IBCs: Metal (31A, 31B and 31N); Rigid plastics (31H1 and 31H2); Composite (31HZ1).
entries.note: A row of the table the corpus's own prose calls table 1 and document order numbers 2 (0044's recorded hazard; see `ib-and-ip-code-authorizations`). Three mapped rows assign IB2. This row is half of the code's rule: the row printed under it states an additional requirement and leaves column 1 blank, and `ib2-vapour-pressure-limit` is that half. The two cannot be one entry, because `evidence` is one contiguous span of one row and the two rows are two units.

entries.name: The additional requirement printed under IB2: a vapour pressure ceiling

locator.citation: § 172.102 table 2, row blank in column 1 below row [column 1 = "IB2"]

ambiguity.question: The row leaves column 1 blank and states an “Additional Requirement”, and the corpus nowhere says what it is additional *to*. § 172.102 states no convention for a blank code cell; the markup carries no rowspan, no grouping and no distinguishing class (measured on 0043); and this row's text is byte-identical to the one printed under IB1, so the words themselves cannot say which code they qualify. That a row blank in the code column continues the row above it is the reader's inference and not the regulation's statement. If it is wrong, every IB2 assignment in the § 172.101 table carries a vapour-pressure ceiling it does not have.

anchor.citation: § 172.102 table 2, row blank in column 1 below row [column 1 = "IB2"]

entries.evidence: | Additional Requirement: Only liquids with a vapor pressure less than or equal to 110 kPa at 50 °C (1.1 bar at 122 °F), or 130 kPa at 55 °C (1.3 bar at 131 °F) are authorized.
entries.note: 0046 records the semantic relationship separately from 0043's structural locator. The regulation never states the blank-cell convention in prose, so `clarity` remains `ambiguous`; 0046 is the explicit `fate: decision` that chooses the well-supported table reading and records this passage as continuing the one direct `special-provision-codes / IB2` definition at `ib2-authorized-ibcs`. The continuation copies neither vocabulary nor term; its structural anchor resolves this row under the IB2 row. The three column 7 cells assigning IB2 already resolve to both entries, and 0044 now mechanically requires both.

entries.name: IB3 authorises metal, rigid plastics and composite IBCs
entries.evidence: IB3 | Authorized IBCs: Metal (31A, 31B and 31N); Rigid plastics (31H1 and 31H2); Composite (31HZ1 and 31HA2, 31HB2, 31HN2, 31HD2 and 31HH2).
entries.note: A wider list of composite IBCs than IB2's, and the difference between the two rows is the whole reason the packing group III acetic acid band takes a different code from the two stronger bands. It is the direct table-2 definition that `ib3-vapour-pressure-limit` continues under 0046; together with that continuation and the table-4 Large Packagings entry, 0044 resolves IB3 to three defining rules.

entries.name: The additional requirement printed under IB3: a vapour pressure ceiling, except for UN2672

locator.citation: § 172.102 table 2, row [column 2 = "Additional Requirement: Only liquids with a vapor pressure less than or equal to 110 kPa at 50 °C (1.1 bar at 122 °F), or 130 kPa at 55 °C (1.3 bar at 131 °F) are authorized, except for UN2672 (also see special provision IP8 in Table 2 for UN2672)."]

ambiguity.question: The same question as `ib2-vapour-pressure-limit`: the row leaves column 1 blank and nothing in § 172.102 says which code an “Additional Requirement” row qualifies. This one is addressable by an ordinary column 2 key only because its trailing UN2672 clause makes its text unique — IB2's is byte-identical to IB1's and needs 0043's selector — and an address is not a reading. The map records both rows the same way for that reason.

anchor.citation: § 172.102 table 2, row blank in column 1 below row [column 1 = "IB3"]

entries.evidence: | Additional Requirement: Only liquids with a vapor pressure less than or equal to 110 kPa at 50 °C (1.1 bar at 122 °F), or 130 kPa at 55 °C (1.3 bar at 131 °F) are authorized, except for UN2672 (also see special provision IP8 in Table 2 for UN2672).
entries.note: 0046 records the same explicit decision as IB2 without replacing this entry's better ordinary row key. The regulation never states the blank-cell convention in prose, so `clarity` remains `ambiguous`; `fate: decision` names 0046 rather than leaving the association unresolved. The primary locator remains the unique column 2 key, while the relation's structural anchor independently resolves that same row below `ib3-authorized-ibcs`. It prints “IP8” and “Table 2” and not “IB3”, so it still carries no direct `defines`; the inherited definition comes only through the anchored continuation. entries.name: IB4 authorises metal IBCs of nine specifications
entries.evidence: IB4 | Authorized IBCs: Metal (11A, 11B, 11N, 21A, 21B, 21N, 31A, 31B and 31N).
entries.note: Metal only, and nine specifications where IB2 names three. No “Additional Requirement” row follows it, which is what makes the two that do follow IB2 and IB3 a reading rather than a layout convention: the corpus prints one where it means one.

entries.name: IB3 also authorises Large Packagings for packing group III liquids

ambiguity.question: A Large Packaging is not an IBC, and § 172.102(b)(4) says an IB code applies **only** to transportation in IBCs. This row is the corpus authorising something else under the same code, and § 172.102(c)(4) says so in terms. The map records the contradiction and chooses neither reading.

entries.evidence: IB3 | Authorized Large Packagings (LIQUIDS)(PG III materials only) 2
entries.note: A separate direct definition of IB3, and the instance 0044 was decided on: a pointer naming only the table-2 IBC rule leaves this Large Packagings rule obliged by nothing. Under 0046 the vocabulary also includes `ib3-vapour-pressure-limit`, so an IB3 pointer owes all three. The row quoted is the table's header row — it carries the code; the inner and outer packagings beneath it are outside this sliced extent.

entries.name: IP1 requires IBCs to be packed in a closed freight container or transport vehicle
entries.evidence: IP1 | IBCs must be packed in closed freight containers or a closed transport vehicle.
entries.note: A row of the IP code table — the corpus's prose calls it table 2 and document order numbers it 3. It is on the Alkali metal amalgam row beside IB4, which is the pair § 172.102(c)(4) describes: the IB code says which IBCs, the IP code says how they travel.
